articles.title: A 75-year-old man from Mandi lost his wife, left home and began living in forest before being rescued and brought to old-age home; years later, he found love and married a 63-year-old woman he met there
articles.summary: KULLU: In an unusual wedding that brought a ray of companionship into two otherwise lonely lives, 75-year-old Kanhaiya Lal and 63-year-old Sabina tied the
articles.body: KULLU: In an unusual wedding that brought a ray of companionship into two otherwise lonely lives, 75-year-old Kanhaiya Lal and 63-year-old Sabina tied the knot at an old-age home in Himachal's Bilaspur district on Wednesday.Kanhaiya Lal, a native of Mandi district, wore a sherwani, while Sabina, originally from Kolkata, dressed in a red saree and exchanged wedding vows in accordance with traditional wedding rituals.The wedding was solemnised at Apna Ghar Old Age Home in Dayoli, where the two had met and gradually developed a bond. The couple exchanged garlands around 11.30 am, followed by traditional wedding rituals. The celebrations began on Tuesday evening with the haldi ceremony. Women residents of the old-age home applied turmeric to the bride and groom and sang traditional wedding songs.Bilaspur DC Kiran Bhadana also attended the ceremony on Wednesday, congratulated the newlyweds and presented them with a shagun. District Welfare Officer Ramesh Bansal and Apna Ghar founder Prakash Bansal were among those present.Kanhaiya Lal, a resident of Thunag village in Seraj area of Mandi district, has been staying at the old-age home for nearly three years. After his wife's death, a distressed Kanhaiya had started living in a forest before being rescued and brought to the old-age home, said an official.Sabina (63) originally belongs to Kolkata. She had come to Shimla a few years back and eventually reached the old-age home. Initially, she was unable to provide details about herself because of her mental condition. After her condition improved, she decided to stay at the institution, said Parkash Bansal."Their acquaintance at the old-age home gradually developed into a relationship, with both deciding to spend the rest of their lives together," added Bansal.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. articles.title: Nike co-founder Phil Knight and wife pledge record $2 billion to cancer research in 2025, building on nearly two decades of donations to transform early detection, clinical trials and patient care
articles.summary: A cancer diagnosis can set off a difficult journey that extends well beyond medical treatment.
articles.body: A cancer diagnosis can set off a difficult journey that extends well beyond medical treatment. Patients and their families often have to navigate unfamiliar healthcare systems, seek access to specialised care and make decisions about treatment options while dealing with considerable uncertainty. At Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), a new philanthropic commitment is intended to address some of these challenges. Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny Knight, pledged $2 billion to the university's cancer research institute, a contribution that could reshape its approach to early detection, clinical research and patient care. The couple's latest commitment also marks a significant expansion of their longstanding involvement in cancer research in Oregon.Phil Knight and wife make record $2 billion cancer research pledge in 2025Announced in August 2025, the pledge is directed towards the Knight Cancer Institute at OHSU in Portland, Oregon. The university described it as the largest single donation ever made to a higher-learning institution in the United States.The funding is intended to help the institute advance its diagnostic capabilities, widen access to innovative clinical trials and make the experience of receiving cancer care less complicated for patients and their families. Rather than concentrating exclusively on laboratory research, the proposed work also addresses the difficulties people encounter while moving through the healthcare system after a diagnosis.For OHSU, the commitment represents an opportunity to expand work across several areas of cancer research and treatment. The institute has indicated that it wants to improve how cancers are identified, develop more targeted approaches to treatment and make promising medical advances more accessible to patients.Phil and Penny Knight said they were encouraged by what the institute could achieve through the initiative, describing its potential impact as extending beyond the university and benefiting humanity.How earlier donations shaped OHSU's cancer research programmeThe couple's relationship with OHSU goes back well before the latest announcement. In 2008, the university named its cancer institute after Phil and Penny Knight following their $100 million contribution. That donation helped establish the foundation for their continuing involvement in the institution's cancer research programme. Five years later, they announced another substantial commitment. The Knights offered $500 million through a fundraising challenge, on the condition that the university raise an equivalent amount within two years. OHSU met the target, allowing the institution to move forward with an expanded cancer research programme.The earlier contributions also helped support developments in early detection. According to Dr Brian Druker, chairman of leukemia research at the Knight Cancer Institute, the funding contributed to the creation of a large-scale programme focused on identifying cancer at an earlier stage.Druker has also credited the cancer challenge with encouraging the development of blood tests designed to detect cancer before it progresses. The institute subsequently expanded its work in precision medicine and targeted therapies, approaches that seek to identify treatments based on the characteristics of a particular cancer.How the institute plans to make cancer care easier for patientsFor someone diagnosed with cancer, getting the right treatment can involve more than finding a specialist or identifying an appropriate therapy. Patients may need to understand complicated medical information, explore clinical trial opportunities and navigate different parts of the healthcare system. This is one of the problems the Knight Cancer Institute has identified as part of its future work. Druker has acknowledged that navigating healthcare after a cancer diagnosis can be particularly difficult, and said the institute intends to change how patients encounter the system.The proposed investment is expected to support improvements in diagnostic technology and access to clinical trials, alongside efforts to simplify the process for patients and their families. Clinical trials are an important part of cancer research because they allow investigators to assess emerging treatments and examine whether new approaches can improve outcomes.The institute's existing work in precision medicine also provides a foundation for its plans. Instead of relying on a single treatment approach for every patient, precision medicine uses information about an individual's cancer to help guide decisions about care.Phil Knight's philanthropy extends beyond cancer researchThe $2 billion commitment is among the largest philanthropic contributions associated with Phil Knight, whose fortune was estimated at $35.4 billion by Forbes at the time of the announcement. Knight, 87 at the time, built his wealth through Nike, the sportswear company he co-founded. He stepped down as its president and chief executive in 2004 before retiring as chairman in 2016. His charitable contributions have frequently supported education, research and institutions connected to his own academic background.The University of Oregon, where Knight studied and competed as a track athlete, has been a major recipient of his philanthropy. Several facilities at the university carry the Knight family name. These include the Knight Library, while its basketball arena honours his son Matthew Knight, who died in a scuba diving accident in 2004.Knight has also supported Stanford University, where he completed his business education. In 2016, he pledged $400 million towards a programme intended to bring graduate students from around the world to Stanford to work on major societal challenges, including poverty and climate change.How the donation compares with other major gifts to US institutionsLarge donations to universities and medical institutions have become an important part of American philanthropy, particularly when wealthy individuals direct substantial portions of their resources towards education and research. In 2018, businessman and former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg pledged $1.8 billion to Johns Hopkins University. The contribution was intended to strengthen financial aid and help students from low- and middle-income backgrounds attend without having to shoulder the full cost of their education. In February 2024, Ruth Gottesman, the widow of financier David Gottesman, donated $1 billion to the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in the Bronx, New York. The gift was intended to fund free tuition for students at the medical school.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Psychology suggests women who love wearing their mother's old sarees may value them for more than just comfort; how the six yards of cloths carry a whole childhood, and an emotional pull from nostalgia to clinging the pallu
articles.summary: Memories of our mothers draping sarees go back to us watching her adore the silhouette on herself, while we watched as little children standing and
articles.body: Memories of our mothers draping sarees go back to us watching her adore the silhouette on herself, while we watched as little children standing and watching her tuck each pleat carefully till it sat perfectly.And today, when we open an old cupboard and a soft cotton catches our eyes from a summer long ago, it brings back the same nostalgia.A silk saved for weddings, a border that looks exactly like it did on your mother's shoulder, all remind us of hiding behind the pallu as a child, or holding on to it in a crowded market.So, when a woman pulls out one of those old sarees and chooses to wear it, it can look like a simple style choice. Sometimes it is. But sometimes there is a lot more folded into that fabric than anyone can see from the outside.This brings us to the question: why does something so ordinary feel so powerful, and how a saree is not just a piece of cloth but actually emotion-laden- six yards of beauty.Here is what that psychology can tell us about a woman, her mother's saree, and the childhood she carries with her.Why some women love wearing their mother's old sareesAccording to researchers at the University of Southampton, nostalgia is a sentimental longing for one's past, and it helps build self-continuity, a sense of connection between who we were and who we are now. In a 2024 paper, researchers also say that nostalgia is directed toward specific objects, and a mother's saree is that basket of memories.Smell can bring memories backA Southampton study on scent found that scent-evoked nostalgia came with more positive emotions than other kinds of memories. Writing on grief makes a similar point. A loved one's clothing often keeps their smell, which can trigger specific memories of that person; similarly, a saree kept in a cupboard for years may carry a trace of that familiar scent.Clothes connect us to our mothersA research paper in the White Rose repository reviewed bereavement writing and found that clothing can help people decide and share memories of someone, or identify with them more closely.It also says that a baby's sense of mother and self is shaped partly through the clothing both of them wear. So, the pallu you clung to as a child was part of how your first bond felt, and when grown up, many women wear their mother's sarees simply to feel close to her.Attached memories add value and make the pieces last longerA paper published in NIFT's e-journal, Product Attachment and Sustainability: Two Facets of the Same Coin by Sareekah Agarwaal and Ruby Kashyap Sood, studied whether owners feel emotional connections to treasured textiles handed down in families, and concluded that attached memories and emotions can help such pieces last longer.It mentions a mother's sari among objects associated with identity. A study of urban Indian women, described by Fibre2Fashion, found that memories evoked by sarees, and sarees received from mothers and grandmothers, carried emotional value. One participant called the saree "a memory box." Another study, from Iowa State University's ITAA, interviewed ten mother-daughter pairs about Banarasi sarees and found themes of sentimental value and emotional attachment.So, for many women, wearing a mother's old saree is a quiet way of staying connected to them and the moments that make them who they are today.You use AI every day. articles.body: ROHTAK: In a chilling display of lawlessness, four youths were brutally shot dead in a suspected gang war at Milan Dhaba on National Highway 9 late last night here.The brazen attack articles.title: Sri Lanka mass grave revives quest for answers to forgotten Muslim massacre
articles.summary: As Sri Lanka’s Tamil separatists fought a deadly war with the army, they also killed hundreds of Muslims.
articles.body:
Kattankudy, Sri Lanka — Fouzul Hinaya has lived for 36 years with the memories of two brothers who were killed in an often-forgotten chapter of Sri Lanka’s brutal civil war.

Now, the 60-year-old sees a flicker of hope. She no longer hopes for justice, but is praying that she might be able to at least bury her brothers with Muslim rituals. “I need to give [them] a dignified burial,” she said, speaking from her home in this eastern coastal city.

Tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, were killed in the war between Tamil rebels fighting for an independent homeland and Sri Lankan forces, which began in 1983 and ended with the Tamil fighters being defeated in 2009. The Sri Lankan military has long faced accusations of war crimes committed against the country’s Tamil population.

The government and many in the nation’s Sinhala majority, meanwhile, have pointed to the bombings and assassinations carried out by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) in cities and villages across Sri Lanka. The LTTE killed then Sri Lankan President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993, and before that, Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi, who had previously sent Indian troops to help crush the Tamil rebels.

But the LTTE also carried out massacres of Sri Lankan Muslims in the early 1990s, starting with targeted killings in the eastern towns of Kurukkalmadam, Kattankudy and Eravur. In many cases, Muslims who were initially abducted never returned. Hundreds of bodies have never been recovered.

Then, last month, a court-appointed archaeological team found skeletal remains bearing cut marks in a Kurukkalmadam mass grave, according to Muazzam Mubarak, the lawyer who represents the victims’ families in the court.

“The priority now is to establish whose remains they are, determine what happened, and keep the families informed,” said Zacky Fouz, assistant professor in the department of political science at International Islamic University of Malaysia.

Among those waiting for a phone call is Hinaya.

Hinaya was one of six siblings. Fouzul Ameer and Abdur Rauff were younger brothers who helped their father, Hayath Mohamed, a logger whose income wasn’t steady, earn enough to support the family.

Ameer used to visit Akkaraipattu, a southeastern town 58km from their home town, to sell readymade garments. On a morning in July, 1990, Ameer packed his bags for that trip. “I never thought this would be his final visit”, Hinaya told Al Jazeera.

While he was returning to Kattankudy, the LTTE stopped him near Kurukkalmadam. Dozens, including Ameer, were gunned down — the death estimates vary from 60 to about 150 people.

For Sri Lanka’s Muslim population, the massacre was a turning point. Sinhalese make up 75 percent of the country’s population, while Tamils and Muslims constitute 15 and 10 percent respectively. Up until the Kurukkalmadam massacre, the LTTE had often abducted Muslims for ransom, using the money it received to fund its fighting. At its peak, the LTTE controlled almost a quarter of Sri Lanka.

Now, it was no longer Muslim money the Tamil rebels were after. They wanted blood.

In August 1990, a month later, the LTTE killed at least 300 Muslims in two mosques in the eastern towns of Kattankudy and Eravur. At the time when Ameer was killed, Abdur Rauff, another of Hinaya’s brothers, was working in a shop in the north of the country.

He returned home to join his grieving family. Days later, he set out from home with a push cart to buy provisions from the nearby town of Batticaloa.

But he was abducted by the LTTE and was never found again. He is presumed dead.

In 2016, Sri Lanka set up an Office on Missing Persons, an independent department to research the fate of missing and disappeared people. Hinaya lodged a complaint with the office, like hundreds of others from all the ethnic groups whose loved ones had been missing since the start of the civil war.

She wondered: could the mass graves that were being searched yield clues? And what’s next?

“Where the evidence supports criminal charges, the authorities should pursue them”, Fouz of the International Islamic University told Al Jazeera.

But with the mass killings, the LTTE took more than lives — it also ruptured a carefully preserved bond between Sri Lankan Tamils and Muslims.

In 1987, after Sri Lanka entered into an agreement with India, a contingent of India’s military was deployed to the country. They were officially there as peacekeepers to help implement a peace deal between Colombo and the LTTE. But they were soon the target of mistrust from both sides.

During their stint in Sri Lanka, residents of several Tamil and Muslim villages in Mullaitivu, part of the Northern Province, were forced to vacate their homes so Indian troops could set up camps there.

“This was our first displacement,” recalled Mohamed Rizni, now 59, who was ejected from his home with his family. But by early 1990, the Indian military departed from Sri Lanka. Rizni and others returned to their villages. “Tamils and Muslims were in harmony. We were like one family and we returned to our villages,” he told Al Jazeera.

That changed in October 1990. “The LTTE gathered all the Muslims in their villages in the Northern Province and informed them to leave the province within two days,” Rizni said.

Rizni was shocked. “We never posed a challenge to Tamils. We just made 5 percent of the Northern Province, while Tamils made more than 90 percent,” he said.

In October 1990, the LTTE forcibly expelled the entire Muslim population of the Northern Province, estimated between 75,000 and 100,000. They were not allowed to take anything with them except clothes. They moved to other parts of the country as refugees. Decades later, Rizni still remembers what the family lost to the LTTE: The rebels took 99 buffaloes, 42 cows, a four-acre coconut estate, an eight-acre paddy field, a house and a grocery shop.

Fouz said the LTTE’s attacks on Muslims showed the exclusionary character of its vision of a Tamil homeland.

“The movement claimed the north and east as a Tamil homeland, yet these provinces were also home to long-established Muslim communities with their own political aspirations and claims to land and belonging,” Fouz told Al Jazeera.

He pointed to the contradiction in the LTTE’s claim to be fighting against Sinhala majoritarianism by reproducing “that same logic of exclusion in its treatment of Muslims”.

In 2009, Sri Lanka crushed the LTTE, bringing the three-decade-old civil war to an end. According to United Nations estimates, nearly 40,000 civilians were killed in the final stage of the war in the Northern Province.

After the war, many Muslim refugees resettled in their villages in the north.

Yet Fouz, the academic, and Rizni, the survivor of two rounds of displacement, said that Sri Lanka had not yet carried out any comprehensive resettlement.

Riyas Farook, a parliamentarian from the ruling National People’s Power alliance, described the killing and the forced expulsion of Muslims in 1990 as serious crimes against humanity.

“No political struggle or ethnic demand can justify killing innocent people or forcing families to leave their homes,” Farook told Al Jazeera.

Farook said he expected authorities would conduct a proper and independent investigation, identify the victims and establish the facts unearthed from the Kurukkalmadam mass grave.

“We fully understand the difficulties faced by northern Muslim families who were forced to leave their homes,” he told Al Jazeera. “Our responsibility is not only to help them return, but also to ensure that they can rebuild their lives with dignity.”

Ultimately, Rizni said, he hoped that the traditional harmony that once marked Muslim-Tamil ties could be revived. “Tamils and Muslims will always have a good relationship. Muslims will not forget the expulsion.”

But for what the LTTE did to Muslims, “we will not blame the Tamils,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Kurukkalmadam mass grave excavation offers one pathway to that closure, Fouz suggested. “How the authorities follow through at Kurukkalmadam,” he said, “will determine whether Sri Lankan Muslims can finally get what they’ve long waited for: answers.”

articles.title: Veruschka, one of world’s first supermodels, dies at 87
articles.summary: The legendary German model, who became a muse to the most influential fashion designers and photographers of the 1960s and 1970s, died in Berlin on Tuesday.
articles.body: Vera von Lehndorff, better known as Veruschka, who, with her towering frame and daring poses became one of the world’s first supermodels, died on Tuesday in Berlin. She was 87. Her death was announced on the website of her sister Catharina Kappelhoff-Wulff’s luxury belt brand. “In the 1960s and 70s she shaped the world of fashion, art and photography like no one else,” the statement said, calling the German model an “extraordinary woman” and “global icon.” Veruschka broke away from conventional ideas of modeling at the time – using her body more expressively and dramatically than her contemporaries, and often becoming an active collaborator during photoshoots. Born in 1939 in Königsberg, then part of East Prussia and now Kaliningrad, Russia, Veruschka was raised on her family’s estate in what is now Poland. She grew up in the shadow of war. Her father, Heinrich Graf von Lehndorff, was a member of the German resistance who was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. Her family settled in Hamburg after the war, where she studied art before moving to Florence. It was there, aged 20, that she was discovered by Italian photographer Ugo Mulas. At more than six feet tall, she stood apart from other models of the era, using her striking features and physicality to create photographs that were dramatic and avant garde. By the mid-1960s, she had become one of the most recognizable and highly paid models in the world, catching the eye of Vogue editor-in-chief Diana Vreeland, who would put Veruschka on the magazine’s cover a dozen times. The supermodel also appeared in several movies, including Michelangelo Antonioni’s “Blow Up” in which she played herself in a famous scene opposite British actor David Hemmings and “Casino Royale” in 2006. In the 1960s and 1970s she worked with the most influential fashion houses and designers – a muse to Valentino Garavani, Yves Saint Laurent and Karl Lagerfeld. Photographer Richard Avedon called her the most beautiful woman in the world. Avedon and Veruschka collaborated on one of the most expensive photoshoots in fashion history. Called “Great Fur Caravan,” the 26-page spread in Vogue was shot over five weeks in Japan, and the publication spent $1 million, today equivalent to about seven times that. Tributes have been pouring in, remembering the supermodel. Italian photographer and former partner Franco Rubartelli, said the two had recently reconnected after more than five decades. “Life gave me a bitter gift: after more than fifty years of knowing nothing of each other, it allowed me to hear from Veruschka once again,” he wrote on Instagram. “And now, just as that door had opened a mere few centimeters after half a century, the wind has blown it shut.” America’s Next Top Model judge and photographer Nigel Barker said Veruschka “helped revolutionize fashion photography.” “I had the privilege of photographing her in 2001,” he wrote on Instagram. “It was a real milestone in my own career. She was the epitome of style and grace and super humble on set with my team. We all learned a lot of what it meant to work with a true icon.” Veruschka stepped away from mainstream modelling in the 1970s, venturing into a career as an artist. Despite her success she told the German newspaper Bild in 2008, “I never wanted to be a model, a meaningless object. “My dream has always been to be able to disappear when I don’t feel comfortable, to be absolutely free.”

articles.title: A Maine family is seeking ownership of 80 acres of land claimed by Canadian timber companies, including JD Irving, arguing that generations of open use, hunting and timber harvesting give them rights under adverse possession laws
articles.summary: A family in Allagash, Maine, is preparing to go to federal court to assert ownership of some 80 acres that Canadian timber companies, including JD Irving,
articles.body: A family in Allagash, Maine, is preparing to go to federal court to assert ownership of some 80 acres that Canadian timber companies, including JD Irving, are claiming. The Kelly family argues that it has openly used and maintained the disputed land for decades, giving it a legal basis to claim ownership under Maine's adverse possession laws. However, the companies dispute the claim and maintain that the property belongs to them, setting the stage for a federal jury trial scheduled for June 2027.Maine family seeking ownership of 80 acres claimed by Canadian timber companiesThe dispute centres on Joseph P. Kelly, his wife, Manda Kelly, and his sister, Cara Merrill, who are seeking legal ownership of the 80-acre parcel in Allagash. According to a report by The County, the three are pursuing the claim as heirs of John Kelly Sr., arguing that their family has openly possessed and worked the property for approximately 90 years.Maine Public, in its November 13 report, noted that Joseph Kelly and his relatives have continued using the land for activities including harvesting wood and hunting since the 1990s. The family also points to historical property deeds as evidence supporting its claim.The central question is whether the Kelly family can establish that its long-standing use of the property meets the legal requirements for gaining ownership through adverse possession.What does Maine law say about adverse possessionAdverse possession is a legal doctrine that can allow a person to obtain title to land owned by another if certain requirements are met for a period of time. In Maine, someone claiming ownership by this method must show that he used the land openly and continuously for at least 20 years, without the owner’s permission.As explained by The County, the Kelly family must show that it knowingly used the property as its own, even though it understood that the land belonged to the Irving interests. Simply visiting or occasionally using the property would not be enough to establish the claim.The family’s lawsuit lists a number of activities that it claims show its control over the disputed land. These include posting No Trespassing signs, painting purple bands around boundary trees, blocking access roads and restricting access during deer hunting season.The complaint also identifies the construction of a pond, timber harvesting, hunting, farming and general maintenance as evidence of the family's continued use. According to the lawsuit, these activities, along with visible boundary markers, demonstrate that the family exercised control over the parcel for generations.The County reported that the boundary was marked by long-standing physical features, including an old red-blazed possession line, marked trees and other signs that the family says it maintained over several decades. These details are expected to form an important part of the ownership dispute.How the Canadian timber companies have responded to the ownership claimThe opposing side is represented by Allagash Timberlands, which claims ownership of the disputed 80 acres. According to Maine Public, the company is owned by four Canadian companies, including JD Irving, and disputes the Kelly family's right to possess the property.The companies argue that they never gave the family permission to enter or use the land for activities such as hunting and timber harvesting. They are seeking a court ruling confirming their ownership and have also filed a countersuit seeking damages from the family for alleged trespassing and timber harvesting.The dispute also involves other members of the Kelly family. The County reported that Regina Kelly, Lance Kelly and Taylor Jo Kelly have separately asserted rights to possess the parcel. Allagash Timberlands has included the relevant parties in its countersuit, adding another layer to the ownership disagreement. The lawsuit also seeks legal costs and attorney fees.The Irving family's extensive timberland holdings in MaineThe involvement of JD Irving brings attention to the scale of the Canadian family's landholdings in the region. According to The Land Report's profile of the Irving family, the business traces its origins to James Dergavel Irving, who established a sawmill, a gristmill, a carding mill and several farms in New Brunswick, Canada.His son, K.C. Irving later acquired substantial timberland holdings in New Brunswick and neighbouring Maine. The family has since become the largest private landowner in Maine, with its business interests closely connected to forestry and timber management.The Land Report's 2026 update states that the Irving family owns approximately 3.2 million acres through Irving Woodlands across Maine and the Canadian provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.The company's forestry operations extend beyond privately owned properties. The Land Report also notes that Irving Woodlands manages approximately 2.6 million acres of government-owned Crown land in New Brunswick under a 25-year forest management and wood supply agreement.When will the federal court decide the ownership disputeThe case is now moving towards a federal trial after initially being filed in Aroostook County Superior Court in Caribou. According to The County, the proceedings were transferred to federal court in April 2026.In late October, Magistrate Judge Karen Frink Wolf issued a schedule setting out the next stages of the case. The defendants must disclose their expert witnesses by December 18, 2026, while the discovery process, during which both sides exchange relevant evidence and information, is scheduled to conclude by March 26, 2027.All parties have been directed to be ready for trial on June 3, 2027. A federal jury is expected to decide the long-running property and boundary dispute.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Muhoozi Kainerugaba: Ugandan president's son angers DR Congo with social media posts
articles.summary: Gen Kainerugaba threatened a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich area in DR Congo in controversial X posts.
articles.body:
The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.

In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.

The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.

The Ugandan government has yet to respond.

The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.

Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.

Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever

The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter

In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.

The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.

They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.

He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.

Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.

Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.

It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.

During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."

The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels , with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.

Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.

"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.

"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".

The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".

It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.

In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.

In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.

The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.

In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

articles.title: A couple bought the Atlanta house where a 1982 arrest led to a landmark US Supreme Court gay rights case; now a city board has approved the plan to demolish it despite the opposition from civil rights groups
articles.summary: A house in Atlanta, Georgia, that became part of American LGBTQ+ history after a 1982 police arrest has been approved for demolition, despite efforts by
articles.body: A house in Atlanta, Georgia, that became part of American LGBTQ+ history after a 1982 police arrest has been approved for demolition, despite efforts by civil rights advocates to save it. The property at 811 Ponce de Leon Place was once home to Michael Hardwick, whose arrest led to a landmark US Supreme Court case challenging the state's sodomy law. Its current owners, Paul and Penny Gutierrez, want to replace the building with a new house and swimming pool, while preservation campaigners argue that the site deserves protection.Atlanta house linked to Michael Hardwick's landmark Supreme Court caseThe property is located in the Virginia-Highland neighbourhood of Atlanta. Although it may appear to be an ordinary residential building, its connection to a major legal battle has made it an important place for LGBTQ+ rights advocates and historians.According to The Advocate, Michael Hardwick was arrested at the house in 1982 after a police officer entered the property and found him engaging in a sexual act with another man. The officer had arrived with a warrant related to a traffic violation, which The Advocate reported was invalid.Hardwick was subsequently arrested for sodomy, which was classified as a felony under Georgia law at the time. The offence carried the possibility of a prison sentence of up to 20 years.The local prosecutor eventually decided not to pursue the charge. However, Hardwick chose to challenge the state law with assistance from the American Civil Liberties Union and other lawyers.The 1986 ruling and its eventual reversalThe legal challenge became known as Bowers v. Hardwick. In 1986, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 in favour of upholding Georgia's sodomy law as it applied to consensual sexual activity between men.The decision meant that the Constitution did not protect a fundamental right to engage in private, consensual same-sex sexual activity under the circumstances considered by the court. It also allowed similar laws across the country to remain in force.CBS News Atlanta explained that Hardwick had initially won his challenge in a US Court of Appeals before Georgia's attorney general took the matter to the Supreme Court. The eventual ruling against him remained in place for years.However, the legal position changed in 2003 when the Supreme Court decided Lawrence v. Texas. The case, brought with the help of Lambda Legal, resulted in the court overturning Bowers v. Hardwick and striking down laws criminalising private, consensual sexual intimacy between adults of the same sex.The reversal made Hardwick's former home an important physical reminder of a legal battle that had shaped the rights and privacy of LGBTQ+ people across the country.Why the owners want to replace the existing buildingPaul and Penny Gutierrez, the current owners, purchased the property in October 2025, according to Axios. Their plans involve demolishing the existing house and constructing a replacement home with a swimming pool.The owners' position has been represented by attorney Stephen Rothman, who has questioned whether the building itself should be preserved because of its historical connection.As reported by The Advocate, Rothman argued that the house had undergone substantial renovations around 2016 and was now considerably different from the structure that stood when Hardwick was arrested.He also raised concerns about the condition of the property, pointing to poorly constructed renovations, black mould and maintenance problems. According to the attorney, restoring the building could cost more than replacing it.The argument is that preserving the location's history does not necessarily require keeping a structure that has changed significantly since the original incident.The owners have also indicated that they would be open to installing a historical marker on the property, allowing visitors to recognise its connection to the landmark case even if the original building disappears.Preservation campaigners are pushing for historic protectionThe demolition proposal has drawn opposition from civil rights advocates, constitutional law experts and local residents who believe the property should be recognised as a historic landmark.CBS News Atlanta reported that the campaign to save the house has attracted support from people who consider it an important part of the country's LGBTQ+ history. Fred Smith, a law professor who has taught the Bowers v. Hardwick case at Emory and Stanford universities, highlighted the importance of being able to connect legal history with an actual location.He argued that visiting the place where an important event occurred can give students and members of the public a stronger understanding of its historical significance.The house is also included in Atlanta's 2023 LGBTQ+ Historic Context Statement, a document identifying locations connected to the city's LGBTQ+ history. However, being included in the report does not automatically give a property legal landmark protection.According to Axios, more than 90 local individuals and organisations submitted objections to the demolition proposal. More than 100 law professors from across the country also opposed the plans.Atlanta's demolition approval leaves the property's future uncertainThe Atlanta City Council unanimously passed a resolution on November 2 requesting that the city's Urban Design Commission begin the process of considering the property for landmark designation. However, the resolution did not immediately grant the house protected status.The Advocate reported that the Board of Zoning Adjustment approved the demolition request on November 5, just three days after the council resolution. Axios also reported that the board approved most of the zoning requests the Gutierrezes needed for their proposed replacement home. The timing has frustrated preservation campaigners, who believe the city should have moved more quickly to protect the property.There is still a possible route to temporary protection. If the Atlanta Urban Design Commission formally issues a notice of intent to nominate the property as a landmark, the city's rules can trigger an automatic 120-day freeze on demolition permits.Fred Smith told Axios that an appeal of the zoning decision was likely, noting the level of opposition from residents, organisations and legal academics.You use AI every day. articles.title: FedEx airplane overruns runway at Miami airport, temporarily closing all but 1 runway
articles.summary: A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to officials.
articles.body: A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to officials. There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m., the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground. By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays. The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis. FedEx said the plane had “an issue upon landing” and that it is coordinating with investigating officials. “We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries,” the company said in a statement. FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. The UPS plane’s left engine flew off and three pilots along with 12 people on the ground were killed. The FAA had approved Boeing’s proposed fix for the MD-11s “after extensive review.” The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before traveling to the airport. “We appreciate our passengers’ patience as we work to safely resume normal operations,” the airport said in a statement. The runway this FedEx plane landed on Wednesday is different than the one the Amazon cargo plane overran in September. But three of Miami’s runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane cleaning crew. The incident also comes less than two weeks after a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at the Miami airport. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident Wednesday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about the situation.

articles.title: 4 dead, 17 missing after six-storey building collapses in Pakistan's Karachi
articles.summary: At least four were killed and 14 others sustained injuries after a six-storey under-construction building came crashing down in Karachi on Wednesday, with
articles.body: At least four were killed and 14 others sustained injuries after a six-storey under-construction building came crashing down in Karachi on Wednesday, with rescue operations continuing on Thursday to locate 17 people feared buried under the debris.The incident took place in the Baloch Colony area of the Pakistani port city. Police said rescue workers had so far pulled 14 injured people from the wreckage, according to the Associated Press.Government official Nasrullah Abbasi said families had informed authorities that 17 people were unaccounted for following the collapse. While rescue teams had initially confirmed one fatality, three additional bodies were recovered during overnight operations.The building was reportedly being erected illegally on a plot designated for residential use. Sindh chief minister Murad Ali Shah had raised concerns about the construction on Wednesday and promised action over the matter.At a high-level meeting on Thursday, Shah ordered the removal of Waseem Shamshad from his positions as Sindh local government secretary and director general of the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA). He also directed that Shamshad's services be returned to the federal government, a statement from the chief minister's office said.Shah further called for a recommendation to the Centre seeking Shamshad's suspension and a formal inquiry into the matter.Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab said the immediate focus remained on rescuing people trapped beneath the rubble, but did not disclose the number of those missing.More than a dozen officials were also removed from their positions on Thursday over alleged negligence, according to a government statement.According to AP, such incidents are frequent in Pakistan, where building regulations are often inadequately enforced and construction firms are known to use inferior materials or flout safety norms to reduce costs. In another such incident, a school roof collapsed in Peshawar in the country's northwest, killing 34 children and a teacher.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Holiday scammers hook older Americans first, then return later to drain their savings, expert warns
articles.summary: Scammers target older Americans with recovery scams and AI deepfakes during the holidays, hitting victims nine times on average, federal authorities warn.
articles.body: As the holiday season gets underway, scammers are targeting older Americans with costly schemes that could deplete their entire life savings, often returning to exploiting the same victim more than once. The risk of elders falling victim to these schemes rises during the holidays. A November 2026 U.S. Secret Service public advisory shared with Fox News Digital stated that scammers consider the season one of their most profitable times of the year. "USSS is better known for its protective mission," USSS Investigative Analyst Bre Whalen, CFE, told Fox News Digital. "Most people are unaware USSS conducts FI crimes investigations throughout the world, such as Operation Maple Star. Because of its partnerships with the banking community, we've developed close contacts over time." Why holidays are lucrative for scammers Federal authorities warn that scammers exploit the holiday rush and heightened emotions as older adults shop online, track packages online, travel and donate to charities. An AARP holiday survey released in November found that 84% of U.S. adults had encountered a scam or fraud attempt ahead of the holidays. Nearly 39% of those who purchased something through an online advertisement said they were scammed, according to the survey. Around 47% received fake package-delivery alerts, while 35% bought or received a gift card with a stolen balance. Americans ages 60 and older reported around $3 billion in fraud losses in 2025, according to an October 2026 Federal Trade Commission report. The agency estimated that older victims lost as much as $119.5 billion last year, with victims reporting only a fraction of the scams. AGING MEANS LEARNING HOW TO PREVENT COSTLY SCAMS TARGETING OLDER AMERICANS Why older Americans are repeated targets The Justice Department reports that scammers target older Americans an average of nine times. After taking money in an initial scheme, fraudsters often contact victims again, posing as officials promising to recover their funds. "Criminals will go back to where the money is," Amy Nofziger, senior director of fraud victim support at AARP's Fraud Watch Network, told Fox News Digital. WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE "It's just why some banks get robbed every single time — the same bank — because the criminals go where the money is, and older adults hold the majority of wealth in the United States." The process can still be challenging, experts said. Winning the confidence of victims can be difficult after they’ve been targeted and scammed. "Victims don't trust or believe what we're saying because they've been coached by these scam centers to not answer law enforcement and think we're not real," Whalen stated. One holiday scam leads to another The Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said that after a successful scam, some fraudsters will share victims' personal information on the black market. This allows other criminals to target the same person, but with different schemes. A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO? For instance, when an older shopper places an order for a fake Black Friday ad or donates to a fraudulent holiday charity site, scammers take their information and place them on "sucker lists." The lists mark these victims as easy targets, with repeated attacks that could ultimately wipe out their life savings. "Criminals are very adept at sharing information," Nofziger said. "A lot of these criminals don't work in isolation. They work in crime rings. Perhaps Criminal A steals from a victim on a Monday, and then five Mondays later, they give or sell that information to Criminal B to try to manipulate them on another scam, knowing they still might have resources available to steal." FAKE FEDERAL AGENTS PUSH SENIORS TO TURN SAVINGS INTO GOLD BARS FOR COURIERS TO COLLECT Recovery scams bring criminals back Promises to recover stolen money or lost funds are one of the most damaging schemes to older Americans during the holiday season. After a victim loses money, another scammer may call and claim to work for a government agency, or pose as an attorney or a fraud-recovery investigator. The caller then promises to investigate the crime, find the money and get a refund. SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO Fraudsters will also exploit tax and financial deadlines while pushing victims to wire an immediate "processing fee" before Dec. 31 to recover lost funds or unlock a refund. Federal authorities warn that legitimate agencies never require upfront fees to recover stolen funds, but victims often fall prey to these schemes when they become outraged and want swift justice. "For the initial victim, they're so angry, they're so upset, they want to get justice for this," Nofziger said. "They think that this is their way out, oftentimes not really understanding that it's just a secondary scam that's happening." AI holiday traps Scammers are exploiting holiday fears with AI-generated emergency calls that mimic relatives and payment-app requests designed to steal money. One scheme, known as the "grandparent scam," happens when criminals pull videos from social media accounts or public sources. They clone a relative's voice using artificial intelligence, and then pose as loved ones asking for emergency funds or Christmas cash. Fraudsters are also using full AI video deepfakes, sometimes posing as physicians, to bilk funds from unsuspecting older Americans. In December 2025, an 82-year-old Florida grandmother lost more than $200,000 to an AI deepfake scam, when someone pretended to be a doctor in a Facebook community focused on autism. The grandmother said she had been saving her money for her autistic grandson’s future, and the fake physician urged people to invest. "It looked completely real — his face, his voice, everything," she told First Coast News. "I wanted to save more money for my grandson, and so I fell for it hook, line and sinker." "I got very emotional and so angry with myself that I had difficulty functioning. I lost 20 pounds and couldn’t sleep because it went through my mind over and over again." How loved ones can help Shame can keep victims silent, which ends up leaving them vulnerable to repeat attacks, Nofziger said, adding that victims may feel guilt for being scammed in the first place. Nofziger urges families to discuss these scams openly, while taking steps to avoid victim-blaming. "The scammers are masters of manipulation, and they know how to manipulate human beings and their feelings," she said. "The victim has been manipulated and technically, you know, brainwashed by this criminal for months and years." "It took years to get there. It might take a long time to unravel that emotional grasp that these criminals have on their victims... The person who should be embarrassed is the criminal who stole the money from them." She added that unraveling a scammer's manipulative hold takes time and outside support, whether from local law enforcement, support groups or counselors. SEND US A TIP Can victims get their money back? Victims are urged to contact their banks, payment providers, and local law enforcement immediately if they suspect fraud. Banks can possibly stop or recall some transfers, but it largely depends on the payment method and how quickly they report the scam. GOT A TIP? Cryptocurrency, gift cards, cash and gold are more difficult to recover since criminals typically know how to move them quickly. Once a victim is ensnared, scammers can move the money through multiple accounts and intermediaries, such as money mules, to hide transactions. USSS advises victims to immediately report any suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "Current fraud info is provided real time; in most cases we have just minutes to act on this information before the fraud is committed," Whalen said. "We work closely with local police and banking industry, although we are still working to make efforts to partner with some of the banking sector that is slow to respond to real-time data." Anyone of any age, including non-members, can contact the free AARP Fraud Watch Network Helpline at 877-908-3360 for guidance, support groups and to learn about other steps to take. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Victims and families can also contact the National Elder Fraud Hotline at 833-FRAUD-11 or visit the Justice Department’s Elder Justice Initiative website.

articles.title: Secret Pentagon UFO hunt drew blueprints for hidden Nevada bunker to store ‘exotic’ materials
articles.summary: Declassified Pentagon records reveal Bigelow Aerospace planned a secret underground vault in Nevada to store recovered UAP hardware and samples.
articles.body: Buried beneath 15 to 20 feet of Nevada earth, behind 3-foot-thick reinforced concrete walls, a steel vault door and a heavily guarded access tunnel, a Pentagon contractor drew up plans to build a 5,000-square-foot subterranean fortress. The bunker was designed to store what was described as acquired "exotic material or tissue" – including recovered hardware and biological samples tied to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), the Pentagon’s broader term for UFOs and other unexplained sightings in the air, space or sea. The blueprint was not drawn from science fiction. It is detailed inside a 538-page declassified contractor report released by the Department of War as part of the Trump administration's latest batch of UAP records, exposing how close a private firm came to building a secure repository under a $22 million Pentagon program. EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL SAYS UAP FILES REVEAL 'TREASURE TROVE' OF INTELLIGENCE DATING BACK TO THE 1940S The vault plans highlight the ambitions behind the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program – also referred to in Pentagon correspondence as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program. Launched in 2008 through a $10 million congressional earmark steered by then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., and the late Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, the effort was billed as a study of foreign aerospace threats out to 40 years in the future. Internal Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) briefing notes from May 2009 say Reid was hunting for radical technological "leaps" across 12 areas – ranging from futuristic propulsion and stealth to directed-energy weapons, space-time travel and how advanced craft affect pilots. Behind closed doors, however, contractor Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) was preparing to acquire and store physical materials. 'NON-HUMAN' BODIES ALLEGEDLY RECOVERED FROM CRASHED UFO, DOCUMENTARY FILMMAKER CLAIMS When the DIA solicited bids in August 2008, only one company applied: North Las Vegas-based BAASS, founded by longtime Reid supporter Robert Bigelow. The DIA awarded the contract the following month. articles.title: Stone Cold Steve Austin hates slow fishing, Trey McKinney hunts geese & Steven Rinella talks turkey
articles.summary: Steven Rinella's wife calls skipping turkey "sinful," but the MeatEater host insists Thanksgiving dinner should feature fresh venison, elk or duck instead.
articles.body: 'Field Notes' is a weekly OutKick OutDoors column featuring the biggest hunting, fishing and outdoor stories, viral videos, reader submissions and whatever else Mother Nature throws our way. It runs every Thursday on OutKick.com. Last year, I struck a nerve with Steven Rinella. Turns out, the MeatEater host has some very strong opinions about what belongs on the Thanksgiving dinner table. And spoiler alert: It's not turkey. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "This … OK. This is a major issue in my marriage," Rinella told me. You see, Rinella considers himself a Thanksgiving purist. "I've pointed out to [my wife] that historians don't even think the Pilgrims ate turkey on the first Thanksgiving. They think they were probably eating geese or ducks," he explained. "They ate the best of what they had. They definitely ate deer meat, you know?" So that's his philosophy. Thanksgiving dinner should be whatever you've recently harvested. Venison, elk, duck — whatever's good and fresh. His wife, Katie, on the other hand, thinks it's downright "sinful" to skip the traditional turkey. But if you are committed to turkey, Rinella thinks you're probably cooking it wrong. According to Steve, roasting a whole bird is one of the worst ways to prepare it. By the time the legs are cooked through, the breast is usually dried out. Or, as he put it, "incinerated." His solution? Break the bird down and cook each part the way it deserves. Smoke the breasts, slow-cook the legs and thighs, and stop trying to make every piece of a very lean animal finish cooking at the same time. And if you're one of those people who thinks turkey is dry, bland and generally inferior to the mashed potatoes? "Not the turkey's fault," Rinella deadpanned. Fair enough. To Rinella’s horror, I’m sure, I come from a bird-in-the-oven family myself. But it was always a treat when my uncle or grandpa would bring home a harvest for the holidays. Hard to beat wild turkey on your plate and Wild Turkey in your glass. But, I'm curious where you guys stand. Are you taking the Rinella approach and serving up venison, elk or whatever happens to be in the freezer? Did you save a wild turkey from spring hunting season? Or are you perfectly content shoving a regular ol' Butterball in the oven and calling it a day? No judgment! Just whatever you do, don't do this: Send me your menus, photos and strongly held opinions at Amber.Harding@outkick.com. Bonus points if you harvested dinner yourself. And with that, let's get into this week's Field Notes. Weekly round-up: rogue bald eagles, lunch-stealing bears & when turkeys attack Stone Cold Steve Austin is an impatient angler & Trey McKinney smokes some waterfowl Stone Cold Steve Austin is retired from the ring these days. Now, he's focused on winning off-road championships and — in his downtime — hunting and fishing. But if the fish ain't biting, Steve ain't happy. Off the track, the late Kyle Busch was an avid hunter and outdoorsman. In fact, before his death in May, Kyle entered Maine's coveted moose permit lottery. His name was drawn in June, and his son Brexton ultimately went on the hunt in his place. So I knew the Busch family had an appreciation for the great outdoors. Still, nothing could have prepared me for the room in Samantha Busch's recent Instagram post. Samantha is asking for book recommendations, but I'm going to need everyone to direct their attention to the furniture for a moment. The chair. The antlers. The walls. That little window. Did somebody commission Fred Flintstone to design a hunting lodge? I have — respectfully — 400 questions about this room, and not one of them is about books. Tomorrow, it's officially time to start decorating for Christmas. If you're like me (and this buck I'm about to show you), you've already started. Like a squirrel determined to pilfer bird seed, be ungovernable. Horse pants! That's it. That's all I have to say. Back in September, just days after Trey McKinney became the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year in history, I caught up with the 21-year-old fishing phenom on "Open Season." And while we talked plenty about bass fishing, Trey made it very clear he had other things on his mind. "I basically make my money fishing to spend hunting," he told me. He explained that once tournament season wraps up, he trades his fishing rods for shotguns and spends much of the fall and winter chasing waterfowl with his buddies. It's how he unwinds after months on the road. Well, Trey wasn't kidding. He just shared a video of himself absolutely hammering geese with Front Range Guide Service. The fish finally get a break, and now the birds have to deal with this guy. Alexa, play "Good Old Dogs and God." Someone's cutting onions in here. 'Open Season': Hannah Graham draws the elk tag of a lifetime This week on "Open Season," I sat down with Hannah Graham, co-founder of Marsupial Gear, to talk about her unforgettable first elk hunt in Arizona. I really appreciated Hannah's honesty in sharing the emotional side of hunting — something that often gets overshadowed by photos of trophy bucks, a freezer full of meat and mounts on the wall. Taking an animal's life comes with a responsibility that no good hunter takes lightly. And Hannah was refreshingly candid about the pressure, self-doubt and emotions that came with that responsibility. It's a side of hunting we don't talk about enough, and I think it's a conversation worth having. Check out our full interview here and don't forget to subscribe: Let's open the mailbag. Call of the wild: big racks and setting suns We want to see your biggest catches, hunting harvests, outdoor adventures and whatever ridiculous thing showed up on your trail cam. Got a great story, a burning question or just something you want to get off your chest? We want that, too. Send it all to Amber.Harding@outkick.com or tag @outkickoutdoors on Instagram for a chance to be featured in Field Notes. Mike V. in Shell Knob, Missouri, writes: Didn't know if you would be interested in pics of the most beautiful sunsets over Table Rock Lake or anywhere I've been. I have been taking them for years and would like to share the view we have. This is one example from a year ago. Keep up the good work and I really enjoyed your new Field Notes. Amber: First of all, I'm always interested in pictures of beautiful sunsets. Hit me with 'em. Anytime, anywhere. The most magical sunset I've (personally) ever seen with my own eyeballs was over Lake Superior in Ontonagon, Michigan. All the pastels were breathtaking, and my photo doesn't even do it justice. This one from Mike, though ... this one's a STUNNER. I went fishing on Table Rock Lake back in late September. It was the first time I'd been there, and it won't be the last. Just a beautiful piece of land and water. No wonder Johnny Morris built his empire there. Next up, our friend Chris Janson sent over this muy grande Texas beauty. articles.title: The quad lives on but risks strategic irrelevance
articles.summary: The headlines during President Trump’s recent visit to Shenzhen focused on his summit meeting with Chinese and Russian leaders, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, at which the three sat as equals. The first-ever trilateral summit of this kind signaled the emergence of a “post-U.S. primacy” era, in which a three-way directorate of great powers is…
articles.body:
The headlines during President Trump’s recent visit to Shenzhen focused on his summit meeting with Chinese and Russian leaders, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, at which the three sat as equals. The first-ever trilateral summit of this kind signaled the emergence of a “post-U.S. primacy” era, in which a three-way directorate of great powers is claiming responsibility for managing global affairs.

Such signaling not only obscured the Quad summit in Manila two days earlier but also may help explain why this strategic coalition of four leading democracies of the Indo-Pacific region — the U.S., India, Japan and Australia — is losing its momentum and perhaps its strategic rationale. The Quad’s core purpose has always been to serve as a strategic bulwark against Chinese expansionism and to uphold a stable Indo-Pacific balance of power.

On his way to Shenzhen, Trump stopped in Manila for barely 21 hours to attend a series of engagements, starting with the Quad leaders’ meeting and immediately followed by a dedicated ASEAN-U.S. special summit. Because of Trump’s tight schedule, the Quad meeting was brief , while the U.S.-ASEAN engagement consisted solely of a “working dinner” held in lieu of a traditional formal summit session.

The Quad summit produced a meager outcome, consisting largely of recycled announcements. Almost every initiative in the joint statement had already been launched or announced at the foreign ministers’ level earlier, from the AI accelerator to the critical minerals framework. However, the summit agreed to convene an inaugural Quad business leaders’ forum early next year in India’s financial capital, Mumbai, and hold the first-ever Quad-coordinated maritime patrol exercise across the Indo-Pacific in 2027.

With Trump pivoting from confronting China to selectively accommodating it, the Quad is becoming increasingly marginal to U.S. strategy and now risks strategic irrelevance. Indeed, the Manila Quad summit stood out for its diluted strategic language on Chinese maritime coercion.

With Trump headed to China, the Quad joint statement, while strongly opposing “unilateral efforts to change existing arrangements through force or coercion,” omitted geographic references to the South China Sea, the East China Sea or the Taiwan Strait. This was a sharp contrast to previous leaders’ summits, including those in Tokyo (2022), Hiroshima (2023) and Wilmington (2024), which devoted detailed paragraphs to specific maritime flashpoints, explicitly condemning militarization of disputed features and interference with offshore resource activities.

Before Manila, no Quad summit had ever been held in a non-Quad country. The Quad leaders were meeting formally after more than two years, largely because Trump’s weaponization of tariffs derailed the 2025 summit that India was to host. Yet the Manila meeting did not even restore the broken hosting rotation by designating a host for 2027.

The Manila meeting thus did little to resolve the Quad’s existential crisis. In fact, the Quad’s marginalization in U.S. strategy is apparent from the Trump administration’s own documents. For example, in the White House’s National Security Strategy , the grouping, once a cornerstone of America’s Indo-Pacific strategy , receives just a single, passing mention, buried in a brief reference to India.

There is a more fundamental reason why the Quad is becoming marginal to American strategy — Washington’s changing strategic priorities.

As Trump adopts a more conciliatory approach to China, including repeatedly referring to a U.S.-China G2 (Group of Two), India’s role in U.S. policy is being downgraded. This is evident not only from the National Security Strategy but also from the 2026 National Defense Strategy , the State Department’s 2026-2030 Strategic Plan and the Pentagon’s dropping of the prefix “Indo” from “Indo-Pacific.”

The Quad was formed essentially to draw India into a larger strategic coalition. The U.S., Australia and Japan already have trilateral strategic arrangements and don’t need the Quad to collaborate. The Quad makes sense only in the context of India, which explains why the world’s most-populous democracy was given pride of place in America’s Indo-Pacific strategy, first unveiled in 2017 .

Today, India’s eroding salience in U.S. policy is weakening the Quad, which seems strategically at a crossroads. With no independent institutional machinery, the grouping remains heavily dependent on Washington’s strategic commitment.

The Quad’s symbolic survival attests to the fact that alliances or coalitions do not become irrelevant only when they collapse. They can still hold meetings, issue joint statements and claim to remain functional while losing their original strategic rationale and gradually decaying. If the Quad continues to lose its strategic purpose, it will become a mere showpiece.

The token summit in Manila, arranged at Trump’s convenience and confirmed by the White House only at the eleventh hour, was intended to convey that the Quad is functionally alive. Yet the optics and mechanics of the summit lent weight to the argument that the grouping is slipping toward a lower-priority, perfunctory exercise.

Rather than treating the Quad as the centerpiece of America’s Indo-Pacific strategic architecture, Washington used the brief huddle with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to check a diplomatic box before Trump headed to China to engage directly with Xi and Putin.

This is a reminder that the Quad’s greatest challenge now comes not from Beijing but from Washington’s own strategic drift. When the country leading the Quad seeks bilateral deals with China, the grouping’s foundational rationale predictably blurs.

The Quad may still survive as a forum while losing its edge as a pivotal strategic counterweight to China’s expansionism.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “Water: Asia’s New Battleground. ”

articles.body: A historic farmhouse in West Goshen, Pennsylvania, has received a temporary reprieve from demolition after a Commonwealth Court judge intervened in a long-running preservation dispute. However, the community group fighting to save the property now faces a November 30 deadline to raise $25,000, a condition that could determine whether the demolition halt remains in place. According to reports by The Philadelphia Inquirer and Vista dot Today, the ruling has given preservationists another opportunity to challenge the property’s planned demolition, but their campaign is far from over. The property, known as Forsythe Farm, occupies approximately 8.5 acres at 905 Westtown Road. Its central structure is a three-storey fieldstone farmhouse accompanied by a stone barn and a private bridge. The house has remained vacant for more than two decades, with years of neglect leaving much of the building in a deteriorated and potentially unsafe condition.Court ruling gives preservationists another opportunityOn November 13, Commonwealth Court Judge Patricia McCullough temporarily blocked the property’s demolition while considering an appeal filed by Save Forsythe Farm, a community organisation seeking to preserve the historic site. The group had previously been denied permission to participate in the lower court proceedings concerning the property’s future. Its appeal challenges that decision, arguing that residents should have been given an opportunity to present their case.The judge found sufficient grounds to consider the group’s challenge, particularly questions surrounding whether it had received proper notice and whether its request to intervene should have been heard. Allowing demolition to proceed before the appeal is resolved could permanently eliminate the very property at the centre of the dispute. However, the temporary protection comes with a financial condition. The group must submit a $25,000 bond to the Commonwealth Court by November 30. The bond is intended to account for costs associated with maintaining and securing the property while the legal proceedings continue.Fundraising campaign faces a tight deadlineThe two-week fundraising window has placed considerable pressure on Save Forsythe Farm. According to the group’s president, Stephen Lyons, supporters had collected slightly more than $7,000 through a GoFundMe campaign as of November 23.The organisation is aiming to raise approximately $35,000 in total, covering the court-mandated bond as well as its legal expenses. Despite the financial challenge, the group hopes the fundraising effort will demonstrate the community’s commitment to protecting the property. Its immediate priority is meeting the bond requirement before the deadline so that the demolition suspension can remain effective during the appeal.Why the farmhouse has become a preservation issueThe property has been owned by Joseph Kravitz since 2003 and has attracted growing concern over its deteriorating condition. West Goshen Township pursued legal intervention in 2025 after repeated safety complaints, including reports of trespassing and urban explorers entering the abandoned buildings.Township officials sought a conservatorship to address the property’s condition and prevent further public safety risks. A conservator was subsequently appointed to assess the site and recommend a course of action. In March 2026, Chester County Judge Anthony Verwey approved demolition, concluding that rehabilitation was not feasible given the extent of the structural deterioration. The estimates presented during those proceedings placed rehabilitation costs at approximately $1.2 million, compared with around $121,600 for demolishing the main farmhouse. Additional costs were also identified for temporary access infrastructure needed to carry out the work. The decision prompted opposition from local preservationists, who argued that the property’s historical significance deserved greater consideration before it was removed.Residents envision a heritage siteSave Forsythe Farm takes its name from John Forsythe, a former owner of the land who lived between 1754 and 1840 and was associated with the establishment of Westtown School. According to historical material published by the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia’s Extant magazine, the farmhouse dates to 1818. Its architectural features and connections to the region’s history have made it an important focus of the preservation campaign.The group hopes to transform the property into a community heritage destination, potentially incorporating educational programmes exploring Chester County’s Quaker traditions, abolitionist history, the Underground Railroad and civil rights. Its proposal involves retaining the historic exterior while renovating the interior, although the building’s extensive deterioration presents significant challenges.For now, the farmhouse’s future rests on the community’s ability to meet the November 30 fundraising deadline. Even if the bond is secured, the legal battle will continue, with the appeal determining whether residents get another opportunity to make their case for preservation.You use AI every day.
